newsitem.title: UK: Sterling claws back losses after UK retail sales.
newsitem.headline: Sterling claws back losses after UK retail sales.

text.p: Sterling clawed back some of its sharp losses on Wednesday, gaining four pfennigs from the previous day's trough after receiving a boost from higher-than-expected retail sales.
January retail sales rose by 0.6 percent month-on-month against forecasts for a 0.3 percent rise and scored a year-on year rise of 4.6 percent against forecasts for a 3.9 percent increase.

"There is fairly robust underlying growth in retail sales still. So the theory that things are beginning to slow down, which in our view has always been exaggerated, may not be right," said Robert Prior, economist at HSBC James Capel.
Sterling turned perkier after the figures and reached a session high of 2.7395 marks. At 1154 GMT, the pound was trading at 2.7395, up nearly four pfennings from its Tuesday low of 2.7023 marks.
Against the dollar, the pound stood at $1.6173 against $1.6033 in late Europe on Tuesday.
"(The gains) are a short-term reflex reaction, rather than some profound underpinning of the currency," said Giles Keating, European economist at CS First Boston.
He said the retail numbers had not altered his stance for interest rates to remain unchanged.

Keating said he expected no rate rises for four to six months. "...And for the year as a whole there is a respectable chance that there won't be rate rises and this figure doesn't alter that at all," he added.
Sterling took a pounding on Tuesday, falling almost five pfennigs to a low of 2.7023 marks as expectations of a near-term rise in British interest rates faded.

Minutes from the January 15 monetary meeting, released on Wednesday, had little immediate impact on sterling as Bank of England (BOE) Governor Eddie George and Chancellor Kenneth Clarke stood their ground on interest rates with George advising the Chancellor to raise rates by a quarter of a point.
The strong retail figures suggest the Bank of England will continue to push for higher rates, though the Chancellor is likely to rebuff them, analysts said.

Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered. said the retail figures were "reasonably healthy and encouraging". Fox said he saw it as significant that George, as shown by the BoE minutes, had pared down his advice regarding a rate rise.
George advised the Chancellor to raise rates by a quarter of a point, and while there was a good case for a half-point tightening the Bank would not press the case.
"That was quite positive," Fox said, adding that it should keep markets reassured.
Economists said George's new stance reflected the fact that he is finally accepting that a stronger pound is acting as a substitute for monetary tightening.
"It is in fact a U-turn," said Keating.

George on Wednesday said the recent rally in sterling would not be sufficient to offset stronger inflationary pressure emerging in 1988, though Clarke said the currency's appreciation persuaded him that interest rates did not have to rise.
Later, Angela Knight, economic secretary to the British Treasury, said there were few signs of inflationary pressures in the pipeline.
"Of course we look at the improvement in sales, the improvement in manufacturing," Knight said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.

"We take into account some of the other factors, like for example, there is very little sign of any sort of inflationary pressures in the pipeline for raw materials and so on, and there is the strength of the pound," she said. She said those are all items that have to be taken into account when deciding the future course of interest rates.
